title: Cellar and Room
premise: Bram Montrose has spent twenty years as a hospice nurse rationalizing the one thing he can't explain: the dying count backwards, from a number only they seem to know, and stop at zero. When his grandmother's funeral brings the family back to the old house, Bram discovers that every photograph taken inside now contains an extra chair — a wooden chair that no one remembers, positioned wherever the camera can see it. As family members begin counting in their sleep, Bram realizes the house is running a tally, and the chair is a seat being reserved. To save them he must uncover what his grandfather did in the cellar in 1968, and the truth — a death the family covered up, a victim the law never touched — forces Bram to choose between protecting his family's name and giving the dead what they're owed. In the end, Bram sits in the chair himself, offers the confession no living witness will give, and the count reaches zero not with a death but with a release: the house empties, the chair vanishes from every photograph, and Bram walks out carrying a memory that was never his to keep.
about_author: D. M. Eriksen is the pen name of a former palliative care volunteer who spent six years sitting with the dying in rural Ohio and swears every word of the counting is true. Eriksen writes horror about quiet houses, family ledgers, and debts that outlive the people who incurred them.

chapters.title: The Backwards Men
chapters.summary: POV Bram. At the hospice, Mr. Okafor counts down from thirty-one over three nights and dies at zero; Bram logs it as coincidence, the way he always has. A new nurse asks what the counting means and Bram says, flatly, that dying people count. Emotional beat: Bram's armor of disbelief established — and the first hairline crack in it.

chapters.title: Grandma's House, Full of Strangers
chapters.summary: POV Bram. The Montrose family gathers to empty grandmother Edith's house after her funeral; aunts argue over china, cousins over money. Bram, the one who actually cared for Edith, feels like a hired hand in his own family. Emotional beat: resentment and grief braided together, the family's fault lines mapped before the house exploits them.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Sorting photographs for the memorial slideshow, Bram finds a plain wooden chair in every picture — 1974, 1989, last Christmas — always facing the camera, always in a spot where no chair stood. His sister Dana sees nothing. He photographs the photographs; the chair multiplies. Emotional beat: the vertigo of being the only witness.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Keeps
chapters.summary: POV Bram. The cellar door, sealed since Bram was a boy, stands unlocked. Inside: a fresh-swept floor, a ring stain on the concrete, and the chair — the actual chair — waiting at the bottom of the stairs. He doesn't go down. Emotional beat: dread without explanation; the house has opened a door it once kept shut.

chapters.title: Dana Counts in Her Sleep
chapters.summary: POV Dana. Bram's sister wakes at 3 a.m. with the number nineteen on her lips and her daughter's hand over her mouth. She tells Bram, laughing it off, but she's moved her kids to the motel. Emotional beat: fear converting to superstition; the family's first open admission that something is wrong.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Bram. In Edith's sewing room, Bram finds a ledger of household accounts with pages torn out — 1968 missing entirely — and a note in her handwriting: 'It wasn't a debt. It was a person.' Emotional beat: the discovery that grandma knew, managed, and hid; grief curdling into suspicion of the dead.

chapters.title: Uncle Roy's Version
chapters.summary: POV Roy, Bram's uncle. Roy, drunk and defensive, tells Bram the family story: grandfather Walter's business partner 'ran off to California' in '68, and Walter built the house's addition with the insurance money. Roy's hands shake. He warns Bram to leave the cellar alone. Emotional beat: the official story delivered by a man who doesn't believe it himself.

chapters.title: Seventeen
chapters.summary: POV Dana's daughter, Nell, age eleven. Nell, who sees the chair in every photo on her phone, starts hearing a man's voice counting under the floorboards — and the voice knows her name. She tells the adults; they blame the motel, the stress. Emotional beat: the child as truth-teller no one will believe; isolation sharpening into terror.

chapters.title: The Count Is Shared
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Family members begin counting in unison in their sleep — same number, same night. Bram records it: seventeen. He calls the number a coincidence and hears how hollow it sounds. Emotional beat: Bram's disbelief finally costing him credibility with himself.

chapters.title: Walter's Workshop
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Behind the garage, Bram pries open Walter's old workshop and finds tools wrapped in oilcloth, a chair leg's worth of raw oak, and a 1968 newspaper: 'PARTNER MISSING, FOUL PLAY SUSPECTED.' The victim's name is Amos Pell. Emotional beat: the horror shifting from supernatural to human — the house isn't haunted by a ghost so much as by a crime.

chapters.title: What Happened in the Cellar
chapters.summary: POV Amos Pell, 1968, in fragmented italic interludes. Amos came to collect what Walter owed him; Walter, panicking over ruin, struck him with a chair leg in the cellar and buried the debt in the floor. Edith knew. Emotional beat: the victim given his voice at last; the reader now knows what the family only suspects.

chapters.title: Sixteen, Fifteen
chapters.summary: POV Dana. The count accelerates — two numbers a night. Nell sleepwalks to the cellar door and scratches at it. Dana, out of options, begs Bram to burn the house down. Emotional beat: panic; the family fractures between flight and fight.

chapters.title: The House Refuses Fire
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram returns with kerosene and the cans empty themselves; the match gutters in still air; the smoke alarm chirps a count. The house is not defending itself — it is insisting on something else. Emotional beat: the realization that destruction isn't the answer; the house wants testimony, not ashes.

chapters.title: Roy Breaks
chapters.summary: POV Roy. Roy, at thirteen, helped Walter pour concrete over the cellar stain and has counted backwards in his sleep for fifty years without knowing why. He confesses all of it to Bram at the kitchen table at dawn. Emotional beat: the cost of complicity across a lifetime; pity replacing blame.

chapters.title: Thirteen
chapters.summary: POV Nell. Nell, the only one the chair doesn't hide from, walks into the cellar and sees Amos — not monstrous, just waiting, sitting in the chair with his hat in his hands. She tells Bram: 'He's not angry. He's just not done.' Emotional beat: the haunting reframed as an unfinished appointment.

chapters.title: The Law Won't Come
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram researches Amos Pell: declared dead, case cold since 1969, Walter dead since 1991, Roy beyond prosecution. There is no legal remedy left — no court, no sentence, no one left to punish. Emotional beat: the theme crystallized; justice outside the law is the only justice on offer.

chapters.title: The Family Vote
chapters.summary: POV Dana. Dana gathers the family and lays out the truth; half want to sell the house and run, half want to bury it deeper. Bram proposes a third option: go back into the cellar and give Amos what he came for — acknowledgment, his name said aloud in the room where he died. Emotional beat: the family's choice between denial and witness.

chapters.title: Ten, Nine, Eight
chapters.summary: POV Bram. The night before, the count runs fast — ten, nine, eight in a single hour. The chair appears in rooms where no one is, in photos taken that afternoon at the motel. The house is coming to them now. Emotional beat: the deadline made physical; no neutral ground remains.

chapters.title: Into the Cellar
chapters.summary: POV Bram. The family descends together. Bram breaks the concrete where Roy shows him, finds Amos's remains and his hat, and speaks the confession the family drafted: Walter's name, the debt, the blow, the burial, the fifty-seven years of silence. The counting stops mid-number. Emotional beat: the climax as act of testimony rather than combat.

chapters.title: The Chair Turns
chapters.summary: POV Amos. In the cellar, Amos rises, sets his hat on, and — for the first time — turns the chair to face the stairs instead of the camera. He looks at Bram, then at Roy, and nods once. The temperature lifts. Emotional beat: release without absolution; the dead accepting witness, not forgiveness.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: POV Bram. They bury Amos beside his mother under his own name, and the coroner reopens the case. That night, every photograph of the house shows an empty room. Bram sleeps without dreaming for the first time in the book. Emotional beat: the exhale; grief finally allowed to be ordinary.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: POV Bram, weeks later. Back at the hospice, a new patient begins counting backwards — from three. Bram sits with her, holds her hand, and this time answers the count aloud with her, all the way down. At zero she smiles and goes. Emotional beat: the ending reframes the opening — the counting was never a curse, only the dead asking to be heard; Bram finally listens.
